extracted.intended_audience: district court judges, magistrate judges, court staff, and practitioners (attorneys) managing or litigating patent cases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for courts and practitioners on early-stage management of patent litigation, covering case assignment, protective orders, claim winnowing and construction, pleadings, jurisdiction/venue, discovery scheduling, stays, and mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Pilot Program case assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent cases filed in Pilot Program districts are initially randomly assigned to all district judges; a nondesignated judge may decline within a set period and then the case is randomly assigned among judges designated to hear patent cases. Program selection criteria required designated judges and limits on declinations in some districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeframes for declination vary by district (e.g., 30 days in most districts; 7 days in W.D. Pa. and N.D. Tex.; 28 days in S.D. Cal.). Districts may designate magistrate judges; courts should use assignment systems to ensure fairness and workload distribution. The FJC studies program effects (expertise, speed, reversal rates, forum shopping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require entry of protective order as early as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Because patent discovery often involves trade secrets and highly sensitive technical and business information, courts should require parties to address an umbrella protective order at the initial case-management conference if not already addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protective orders prevent disclosure of sensitive technical, financial, licensing, or business strategy information and often must be in place before meaningful discovery. Courts should preferably enter protective orders early to avoid delays in document production and disputes later in the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multitiered protective orders (tier structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Protective orders may adopt tiers such as: (1) Confidential (Rule 26(c) protection), (2) Highly Confidential—Attorneys' Eyes Only (extremely sensitive; disclosure would create substantial risk of serious harm), and (3) Highly Confidential—Source Code (extremely sensitive source code and related technical material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define who may access each tier: Confidential may be disclosed to parties/representatives who sign an acknowledgment; Attorneys' Eyes Only limited (often excluding in-house competitive decision-makers); Source Code access governed by strict inspection procedures. Courts may tailor tiers to case needs and resolve asymmetric interests by discussing expected productions with parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default protective orders and timing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Some districts implement default protective orders that take effect automatically at case outset; others require produced materials to be treated as 'outside attorneys' eyes only' until a protective order is entered; some provide templates/guidelines for parties to model orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automatic default orders (e.g., N.D. Ill., N.D. Cal.) prevent confidentiality disputes from delaying discovery and permit earlier exchanges required by local patent rules. Where default orders are not automatic, sample orders and source-code guidelines (e.g., D. Del., D. Minn.) help parties craft case-specific orders with predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution bars in protective orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution bars limit the ability of persons who have seen designated material to engage in patent prosecution or post-grant proceedings for a specified time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include prosecution bars where appropriate to prevent misuse of confidential technical information in prosecution. Considerations (discussed elsewhere in the Guide) include duration, scope, and whether the bar is necessary given case circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phased claim winnowing (limits on asserted claims and prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a phased process to limit the number of asserted claims, prior art references, claim terms to be construed, and accused products—typically with initial 'preliminary election' and later 'final election' stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Federal Circuit Advisory Council Model Order (example): Preliminary Election no more than 10 claims per patent and total 32 claims (not later than 40 days after certain document production); Final Election not later than 28 days after Claim Construction Order identifying no more than 5 claims per patent and total 16 claims. Parties may propose lower/higher limits based on case-specific factors (commonality, number/diversity of accused products, technology complexity). Courts should ensure opportunity to add claims presenting unique liability/damages issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of accused products and prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: Phased limitation of accused products and prior art references reduces litigation complexity and cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing asserted prior art and accused products can reduce expense and trial complexity but may unduly impair a defendant's ability to contest validity; the court should balance proportionality and fairness when setting limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of disputed claim terms and meet-and-confer
rubrics_metrics.description: Require parties to identify to each other the claim terms they propose to be construed and the intrinsic/extrinsic evidence they intend to rely upon, then confer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This step narrows disputed terms, focuses issues, and prevents last-minute changes, but meeting and conferring may extend the time needed for claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint claim-construction statement submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Require a joint claim-construction statement listing stipulated constructions, each side's proposed constructions for disputed terms, and the evidence (intrinsic and extrinsic) on which they rely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps focus disputes, provides the court a roadmap for briefing, reduces repeated changes in positions, and aids judicial efficiency. May leave some disputes unresolved, delaying parties' ability to evaluate merits; phased approaches can mitigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-construction briefing procedures (page limits/simultaneous briefing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt briefing rules such as page limits and simultaneous opening and opposing briefs without replies to constrain and structure claim-construction submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such procedures can reduce unnecessary material and speed resolution, but may prevent parties from fully addressing each other's arguments if meeting/conferring was inadequate. Courts should choose procedures mindful of fairness and thoroughness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technical tutorials
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow technical tutorials—either in-person or submitted (paper/multimedia)—to provide the court context about the asserted technology prior to detailed claim-construction briefing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tutorials, especially recorded ones, give the court useful background, can be part of the appellate record, and assist new clerks; they increase burden and cost and parties may present biased depictions. Recording and sharing tutorials can preserve context for later readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequencing claim construction relative to other motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, claim construction should precede summary judgment, though in some cases they may be combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early construction helps clarify issues for summary judgment and trial; combining stages can be appropriate when efficient, but sequenced construction often better frames subsequent dispositive motions and discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary claim construction for preliminary injunction motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary injunction motions usually require a preliminary construction of at least the key claim terms implicated by the injunctive relief request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because injunctions hinge on likely success on the merits, courts should identify and construe terms needed to assess infringement and validity at the preliminary stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step-wise winnowing (before construction, after construction, before trial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply staged limitations: initial limits on asserted claims before claim construction, further limits following claim construction, and final trimming before trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows plaintiffs to refine theories as discovery and construction proceed while controlling complexity and preserving ability to add claims with unique issues. Courts should ensure the process is not arbitrary and preserves parties' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing requirements for infringement plaintiffs
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringement plaintiff must hold all substantial patent rights to sue; must join all joint patent owners; exclusive licensees may need to join licensors in some circumstances; nonexclusive licensees generally lack standing; conveyance of the right to sue requires transfer of substantially all patent rights; covenants not to sue can moot controversies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should examine ownership/assignment facts early and resolve meritorious standing motions; defective ownership or license arrangements can lead to dismissal or require joinder of necessary parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaratory-judgment plaintiffs and assignor estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for declaratory-judgment plaintiffs differ; assignors may be estopped from seeking declaratory judgment of invalidity; parties in privity with assignor may also be estopped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an actual case or controversy exists for licensees and whether assignor estoppel bars certain actions; consider nuances of privity and prior representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant standing and joinder issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant-side standing issues include who is a proper defendant for infringement and declaratory-judgment counterclaims, and joinder questions when multiple parties or related entities are involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve joinder early to avoid multiplicity of suits; examine whether parties should be joined as defendants based on alleged conduct and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading requirements for infringement and willfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleadings must state infringement adequately; willful infringement claims implicate issues such as opinions of counsel and related privilege considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should evaluate sufficiency of pleadings; willfulness allegations may require particular facts supporting a claim of deliberate or reckless behavior and affect discovery (e.g., opinions of counsel). Privilege issues must be handled carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading defenses: invalidity and unenforceability (inequitable conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity and unenforceability defenses must be pled with appropriate specificity; inequitable conduct requires pleading with particularity; privilege issues may arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Rule 9(b) or other heightened pleading standards where applicable; courts should balance adequate notice to the patentee against unfair fishing expeditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory and noncompulsory counterclaims
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between compulsory counterclaims (must be pleaded in the action or may be waived) and noncompulsory counterclaims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should assert compulsory counterclaims early; courts should identify and address potential waiver issues at the pleading stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap with nonpatent claims and choice-of-law issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent cases often involve parallel nonpatent claims (e.g., unfair competition, antitrust) raising choice-of-law and preemption issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should consider whether state-law claims are preempted by patent law (and how ITC or PTO rulings may affect state-law claims) and coordinate such issues early to streamline the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with other proceedings (bankruptcy, ITC, PTO reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent district court cases frequently overlap with bankruptcy proceedings, ITC actions, and PTO review (reexamination, reissue, AIA post-grant review), requiring consideration of stays and coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stay requests carefully (e.g., pending PTAB review, AIA review, CBMR), weighing factors such as simplification of issues, prejudice, timing, and dispute-specific concerns. Consider effects of ITC rulings on district-court proceedings and potential stays relating to parallel proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 11 presuit investigation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 11 requires an objective, good-faith basis for filing pleadings—presuit investigations must be reasonable and factual basis must exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should enforce Rule 11 to deter baseless patent suits; encourage counsel to perform adequate presuit investigation and to withdraw or amend pleadings lacking factual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal and subject-matter jurisdiction and venue considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess personal jurisdiction, original and supplemental subject-matter jurisdiction, and venue early; handle venue transfer motions and consider multidistrict coordination where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early jurisdictional/venue rulings affect where and how the case proceeds; courts should address transfer motions and MDL/coordination early to minimize inefficiencies and forum-shopping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling and case-management conference (CMC) checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Use CMC to set schedule, address specialized issues (protective orders, claim construction timing, discovery limits), and apply an initial case-management checklist to identify salient issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CMC should cover scheduling choices and their consequences, discovery sequencing, claim-winnowing plans, and whether to schedule a Markman hearing. Appendices provide sample checklists and model scheduling orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address multidefendant and multi-patent 'mega' cases early
rubrics_metrics.description: Special management required for multidefendant and multipatent litigations, including standards-compliance suits, customer/manufacturer relationships, and strategies for grouping defendants and limiting claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider limiting claims, grouping defendants, phased approaches, and special discovery plans to control complexity and costs in mega cases. Courts should be attentive to fairness across defendant groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early attention to spoliation issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Spoliation risk and preservation obligations should be addressed at the outset to avoid loss of critical evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issue preservation orders early, communicate preservation obligations to parties, and sanction spoliation where appropriate to deter misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early motions practice (§ 101 subject-matter, indirect infringement, willfulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should be prepared to adjudicate early motions such as § 101 ineligibility, motions to dismiss indirect infringement or willfulness claims, and other dispositive motions that can simplify the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the timing and impact of early motions; some motions may meaningfully streamline the case while others may be premature if claim construction and discovery are incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss damages theories and proof at the outset
rubrics_metrics.description: Require parties to identify damages theories and the proof they will rely upon early in the case-management process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early focus on damages issues can inform claim-winnowing decisions and settlement prospects, and allow targeted discovery on economic and technical issues relevant to damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address proportional scope of discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery in patent cases should be proportional to the needs of the case considering stakes, complexity, and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should tailor discovery to be proportional, taking special care with voluminous technical materials and source code. Use local patent rules and scheduling to manage scope and burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement and mediation processes and considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage resolution through mediation; address initiation, mediator selection, scheduling, mediator powers, confidentiality, relation of mediation to litigation schedule, and mediation in multiparty/multijurisdictional cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should promote mediation early where appropriate, select qualified mediators, define mediator powers and who must attend, and ensure mediation confidentiality. Tailor mediation procedures for multiparty and cross-jurisdictional disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors affecting likelihood of settlement for case categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize categories of patent cases with differing settlement prospects and identify factors (e.g., strength of claims, damages exposure, complexity) that affect settlement likeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case categorization to prioritize settlement resources and tailor mediation strategies; consider whether early claim construction, damages narrowing, or phased proceedings will encourage settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediation evaluation criteria (attorneys, mediators, parties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use structured evaluation forms to assess mediations with items such as mediator preparedness, clarity of process, mediator's ability to generate options and move parties toward settlement, knowledge of law, fairness, length, outcomes, bias, and cost impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect anonymous evaluation data to improve mediation programs. Forms use Likert scales and solicit qualitative feedback on why cases did/did not settle and willingness to use mediator/program again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default standard for access to source code (District of Delaware)
rubrics_metrics.description: When no agreement exists, source code inspection procedures include: single electronic copy on a stand-alone, password-protected computer supplied by the source code provider; placement with an independent escrow agent; access limited (typically to two outside counsel and two approved experts); prohibition on printing/copying without agreement; manifest listing files and MD5 checksums; required utilities for viewing/searching/comparing; and inclusion of build scripts if court finds missing files issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedures ensure secure, controlled access to source code while balancing the producing party's confidentiality concerns and the inspecting party's need to analyze code. Costs for escrow agent to be shared; court may select agent if parties cannot agree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for challenging confidentiality designations and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may request changes in designation of 'Confidential' or 'Confidential - Attorneys' Eyes Only'; documents remain designated until change is completed, and the party asserting confidentiality bears the burden of proving the scope of protection under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require notice to affected third parties when challenging designations and move the court for relief if parties cannot agree. Temporary treatment prevents premature disclosure while disputes are resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return, destruction, and retention of confidential materials after termination
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 60 days of termination (including appeals), parties must destroy or return documents designated Confidential and certify compliance; attorneys may retain a set of court filings and correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should enforce timelines for return/destruction and allow limited retention for attorney files. The protective order should include procedures for removal and destruction of Confidential materials from the Clerk's office after appeal periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification and survival of protective orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Any party may apply to the court for modification of a protective order; obligations under the protective order survive termination of the action and the court retains authority to modify confidentiality provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should permit case-specific tailoring and modifications in light of changing circumstances, and ensure obligations continue after case end to protect sensitive information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written assurance for individuals accessing confidential materials (Exhibit A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals granted access to Confidential materials must sign a written assurance acknowledging the Protective Order, agreeing not to divulge documents, returning materials after termination, and submitting to the court's jurisdiction for enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a standardized written assurance form to ensure all non-attorney reviewers understand obligations and potential sanctions for violations; require prompt return of materials (no later than 30 days after final termination) and include perjury/jurisdiction language.
